description: Our team has been working together for a long time, combining a balanced skill set in programming, data analysis, and design. We aim to build intelligent, visually compelling, and socially beneficial digital products.
summary:
After the destruction of Ukraine’s Kakhovka Dam in 2023, the former reservoir began transforming into a new landscape. We wanted to track these changes using NASA–ISRO's NISAR satellite, but strong radio interference made the images difficult to analyze.
To solve this, we developed a method that reduces radio interference and detects real changes in the landscape without confusing them with errors in satellite data.
We analyzed 22 NISAR images collected between June and November 2026. Before applying our method, standard analysis incorrectly marked 98.2% of the area as changed. Our approach reduced this to 13.7%, with results supported by independent satellite observations.
We also created an interactive website where users can compare images before and after processing, explore detected changes, and see how the landscape has evolved over time.
Our solution helps turn satellite data affected by interference into useful information. Beyond Kakhovka, this approach could support environmental monitoring in other regions where satellite observations face similar challenges.
details:
The Problem: When Satellites Cannot See Clearly

In June 2023, the Kakhovka Dam in Ukraine was destroyed, causing one of the largest environmental changes in the region. As the reservoir drained, areas that had been underwater for decades became exposed. Over time, vegetation started growing, new waterways formed, and the landscape continued to change.

Monitoring these changes is important for understanding how the environment is recovering and how the former reservoir is developing.

We decided to study this area using data from NISAR, a satellite mission developed by NASA and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

Unlike regular optical satellites, NISAR uses radar to observe Earth's surface. This allows it to collect information during the day and night, even when the sky is covered by clouds.

However, we encountered a serious problem.

The NISAR images of the Kakhovka region contained strong radio frequency interference (RFI). This interference appeared as large bright spots covering areas tens of kilometres wide. It made water look brighter than expected and created differences between images that were not caused by actual changes on the ground.

When we applied a standard change detection method to the original images, 98.2% of the study area was marked as changed.

The problem was not that almost the entire landscape had changed. The problem was that the analysis was detecting radio interference instead of real changes.

Rather than switching to a different region, we decided to find a way to work with the affected data.

Our Solution

We developed a method that can reduce radio interference in NISAR satellite images and identify real changes in the landscape.

Our solution has three main parts:

1. We estimate how much interference affects each area and reduce its influence on the satellite images.

2. We developed a statistical test that considers interference when deciding whether the surface has changed.

3. We created a web application where users can explore the processed satellite images and detected changes.

The main idea is simple: instead of treating every difference between satellite images as a real change, our method first considers how much of that difference could be caused by interference.

Data and Study Area

We analyzed 22 NISAR L2 GCOV satellite images collected between June and November 2026.

The images cover approximately 140 × 100 km, including the former Kakhovka Reservoir, the Dnipro River and surrounding agricultural land.

We used observations from two independent satellite tracks:

- Track 143_A_025: 11 images collected from June 24 to November 3, 2026.

- Track 108_D_065: 11 images collected from June 21 to October 31, 2026.

The two tracks observed the same area from different directions, with approximately three days between matching observations. This allowed us to check whether detected changes appeared in both sets of images.

We also used additional satellite datasets, including OPERA DSWx-S1, JRC Global Surface Water, ESA WorldCover and Sentinel-2 imagery, to understand the landscape and validate our results.

Step 1. Understanding the interference

We also found that interference usually covers large areas, around 30–60 km wide, while many real changes occur at a much smaller scale, such as individual agricultural fields.

This difference helped us separate interference from actual changes.

Step 3. Detecting real changes

Cleaning the images was only part of the solution.

Simply removing interference and applying a standard change detection method could still produce false results, because measurements affected by strong interference remain less reliable.

In simple terms, our test trusts cleaner observations more and gives less weight to observations affected by strong interference.

This allows us to identify changes without automatically treating interference as evidence that something happened on the ground.

We also use a 5% false discovery rate threshold to control the number of false detections.

Results and Validation

We tested our solution using real NISAR observations, independent satellite tracks and simulated data.

The results showed a major improvement compared with standard methods.

Change detection results:

Our method reduced the number of areas incorrectly identified as changed because of interference.

In locations where interference was more than ten times stronger than the actual signal, the standard method marked 100% of pixels as changed. Our approach reduced this figure to just 3.4%.

We also tested the method on simulated data where the correct results were known. The new test kept false alarms at approximately 2.7–5.1%, depending on interference strength, while successfully detecting most simulated changes.

To make sure our method was identifying real changes, we compared results from two independent NISAR satellite tracks.

For agricultural fields, the same changes appeared in both tracks four times more often than would be expected by chance. We compared the tracks pixel by pixel: at the scale of tens of kilometres the interference patterns look alike in both tracks, so only field-level agreement counts as evidence. The first-change dates on cropland also matched within 12 days for 50% of pixels, against 26% by chance.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The same window in two tracks and their agreement" ]

We also compared changes in the former reservoir with independent water maps derived from Sentinel-1.

Areas where water appeared or disappeared were identified as changed approximately twice as often as areas that remained dry.

These comparisons support the conclusion that our method detects meaningful changes in the landscape rather than simply following interference patterns.

Interactive Web Application

We wanted our results to be understandable and accessible, not only to researchers but also to people without experience in satellite data analysis.

That is why we created an interactive web application.

Users can:

- Compare original and processed NISAR images using a before-and-after slider.

- Switch between different satellite observation dates and tracks.

- Explore maps showing where changes were detected.

- See when the first detected change occurred in different locations.

- Compare results from two independent satellite tracks.

- Explore interactive charts and statistics explaining the results.

The application allows users to see how interference affects satellite images and how our method improves the results.

Instead of only presenting numbers, we provide a visual way to explore the research.

What Makes Our Project Different?

The main innovation of our project is that we do not simply try to make satellite images look better.

We developed a way to account for interference during the analysis itself.

Many approaches rely on removing noise before processing satellite data. However, when interference is extremely strong, cleaning alone may not be enough.

Our solution combines interference estimation with a statistical test that understands the uncertainty caused by interference.

Another important feature is that our method works with publicly available NISAR L2 GCOV products. It does not require access to the original raw radar signal or additional ground-based calibration equipment.

We also used two independent satellite tracks to validate the results, rather than relying only on the appearance of the processed images.

Finally, we chose to study a real environmental problem in Ukraine, where monitoring landscape changes is particularly important.

Challenges and Limitations

During development, we tested several approaches that did not produce reliable results.

For example, simply subtracting the interference and applying a standard change detection test still produced too many false detections.

We also discovered that some water reference maps could incorrectly identify agricultural fields as water. Because of this, we carefully limited where these datasets were used for validation.

Our final method was developed through repeated testing and comparison with independent observations.

When interference becomes extremely strong, some information cannot be recovered reliably. In these situations, our method becomes more cautious and may miss some real changes rather than report false ones.

The method has also been tested on one region and one observation season. Further research is needed to confirm how well it works in other locations.

Because the study area is affected by the war in Ukraine, we also considered the safety of publishing our results. Our public application does not show detailed interference source maps or attempt to identify their locations.

Impact and Future Development

Our project demonstrates that satellite data affected by strong radio interference can still be valuable.
For the Kakhovka region, this creates new opportunities to monitor how the former reservoir is changing, including vegetation growth, agricultural activity and changes in water coverage.

More broadly, the method could help researchers and environmental organizations analyze satellite observations in other regions affected by radio interference. This is particularly important because satellite monitoring is often needed in places where collecting information on the ground is difficult or dangerous.

In the future, we plan to improve the identification of different types of changes using Sentinel-2 and HLS optical imagery, analyze additional NISAR satellite tracks, and test our approach in other regions.

Our goal is to make satellite observations more reliable and useful, even when the data is far from perfect. By turning heavily affected radar images into meaningful maps, we hope to support better environmental monitoring and show how space technology can help us understand changes happening on Earth.
